title: Vanadium paints one solution in four colours, and that’s how it got its name

cover.alt: A tall glass beaker of dark brown liquid with a tea bag hanging in it, against a white background.

body: Vanadium atoms can give up different numbers of electrons, and in water each of these oxidation states has its own colour: **yellow-orange** for +5, **blue** for +4, **green** for +3 and **lilac** for +2. Add a metal that hands over electrons, such as zinc, and a vanadium(V) solution is reduced one step at a time, so it changes colour again and again. In this film the solution starts as a reddish-brown vanadium(V) complex, and a tea bag of granules of Devarda’s alloy, a mix of aluminium, copper and zinc, does the reducing. Around 1830 the Swedish chemist Nils Gabriel Sefström named the element after **Vanadís**, a Norse goddess of beauty, because its compounds are so beautifully coloured.

slides.alt: A tea bag of metal granules hangs in a beaker of dark brown liquid. The liquid turns olive, then bright sky blue, then green, then greyish blue, and finally a pale violet.
slides.caption: A tea bag of metal granules reduces vanadium step by step: dark reddish-brown turns blue, then green, then violet. This excerpt is sped up 3.5×.
slides.credit: Deni Ingilizovski · CC BY-SA 4.0 · excerpt, sped up 3.5×

slides.heading: Match each vanadium ion to its colour
slides.explanation: Each step down takes one more electron. Zinc can reduce a vanadate solution through all four colours in turn.

events.text: Andrés Manuel del Río finds it in a Mexican ore
Told it is just impure chromium, he takes his claim back
Nils Gabriel Sefström rediscovers it and names it vanadium
Henry Roscoe makes the pure metal

slides.heading: About 85 of every 100 tonnes of vanadium go into steel
slides.note: Mostly as ferrovanadium; the Ford Model T’s chassis used vanadium steel to save weight

slides.question: Del Río first called the element panchromium. What does that mean?
slides.explanation: From Greek for “all colours”, for its wide range of coloured salts. He later renamed it erythronium, “red”, because most of its salts turned red when heated.
